title: Cap. IV: Garissoles one reatus; Helvetic cities decree; in et cum Adamo
pass_a_gloss: The same D. Garissolius silently approves Placeus when he often affirms that the guilt from Adam's sin and from the vice inhering in us are not two distinct guilts but one and the same rising from both — Cap. IX and Cap. XXVII. For if immediate imputation of Adam's sin is posited, two distinct guilts are necessarily posited: one from Adam's sin, one from the inherent vice — the former before hereditary corruption, the latter after; prior and posterior to the inherent vice; cause and rather effect of corruption; the penalty of the one is the inherent vice, not of the other; alien sin outside us versus our own inhering sin; numerically one common sin versus many proper sins; hanging on God's will alone versus on the nature and demerit of inborn corruption; existing before those to whom it is imputed versus only afterward. How then can they not be two distinct guilts amid so many differences? Hence Placeus does not clash with the Decree of the four Swiss evangelical cities Garissolius appends to Charenton. Either they praise the Charenton Decree, with which Placeus agrees, or they give this reason: those who sinned in and with Adam have Adam's sin justly imputed — which Placeus owns as most true. But what is it for us to have sinned in and with Adam? That Adam's sin is imputed to us? So Garissolius takes Cap. VIII. Yet that makes the theologians prove imputation by imputation — a trifling he will not pin on so grave a Decree. By a like phrase: to have been in and with Adam means Adam's being communicated by natural propagation, not imputed; so to have sinned in and with Adam means Adam's sin communicated by natural propagation — whence it is justly imputed, but by mediate or consequent imputation, which Placeus constantly holds.
pass_b_english: The same D. Garissolius silently approves Placeus's judgment when he several times affirms and presses that the guilt from Adam's sin, and from the vice inhering in us, are not two distinct guilts, but one and the same guilt rising from both — chapter 9, section 7, page 190, and section 15, page 306, and chapter 27, section 30, page 809, and so on. For once immediate imputation of Adam's sin is posited, two distinct guilts are necessarily posited, of which one rises from Adam's sin, the other from the vice inhering in us: the former precedes hereditary corruption, the latter follows; the former is prior to the inherent vice, the latter posterior; the former is the cause of corruption, the latter rather its effect; the penalty of the former is the inherent vice, of the latter not so; the former is of another's sin and of a sin seated outside us, the latter of our own sin inhering in us; the former is common to all human beings by numerical identity of the sin, the latter is of many sins in number, and each human being's own; the former hangs on God's will alone, the latter on the very nature of the corruption born in us and on its natural demerit; the former was earlier than those to whom it is imputed, the latter on the contrary was not except afterward. How, then, can they not be two distinct guilts, between which so many and so great differences can be noted?

From this it is plain that Placeus's judgment in no way fights with the Decree of the four evangelical cities among the Swiss, which D. Garissolius appends to the Charenton Decree. For either they praise the Decree of the Charenton Synod, with which Placeus's judgment, as I have already proved, agrees; or they give the reason why they praise it in these very few words: For those who sinned in Adam and with Adam, Adam's sin is justly imputed to them — which proposition Placeus acknowledges to be most true. For it is truly equitable that those who sinned in and with Adam should have imputed to them the sin they committed in him and with him. It is just that a common sin have a common imputation. But what is it that we sinned in and with Adam? That Adam's sin is imputed to us? So D. Garissolius takes it in chapter 8, section 21. For how, he says, could those who existed many ages later have already sinned before in another, unless because he performed that act which is so reckoned of posterity as if they themselves had committed it? And he adds that the theologians, when they teach that we have satisfied in Christ, mean nothing else than that Christ's satisfaction is imputed to us. This interpretation of his fits what he often presses: that Adam's sin is ours only by imputation. From this it follows that we did not sin in and with Adam except imputatively. But then the reasoning of the most learned theologians would turn out trifling. For they would prove the same by the same — the imputation of Adam's sin by the imputation of Adam's sin — which trifling, especially in so grave a Decree, it is wrong to assign to them. What, then, does that phrase mean? It can be understood from a like case. For if someone said that we were in and with Adam, the sense would be not that Adam's being is imputed to us, but that Adam's being was communicated to us by natural propagation. So when we are said to have sinned in and with Adam, the sense is not that Adam's sin is imputed to us (for that would be, as I said, to import a trifling into the Decree of most excellent men), but that Adam's sin was communicated to us by natural propagation. From which it follows that it is justly imputed to us — but by mediate or consequent imputation, which Placeus constantly acknowledges and holds.
source_text:
Idem D. Garissolius sententiam Placei tacite probat, cum aliquoties affirmat et inculcat reatum ex peccato Adae, et ex vitio nobis inhaerente, non esse duos reatus distinctos, sed unum eundemque reatum ex utroque consurgentem — Cap. IX. §. vii. pag. 190. et §. xv. p. 306. et Cap. XXVII. §. xxx. p. 809. etc. Posita enim imputatione peccati Adae immediata, ponuntur necessario duo reatus distincti, quorum unus ex peccato Adae, alter ex vitio nobis inhaerente consurgit: ille antecedit corruptionem haereditariam, hic sequitur; ille prior est vitio inhaerente, hic posterior; ille causa est corruptionis, hic potius effectum; illius poena est vitium inhaerens, huius non item; ille est peccati alieni ac extra nos siti, hic est peccati nostri, nobis inhaerentis; ille est omnium hominum communis identitate numerica peccati, hic est multorum numero peccatorum, et suus cuique homini proprius; ille pendet a sola Dei voluntate, hic ab ipsa corruptionis nobis innatae natura et naturali demerito; ille prius fuit quam ii essent quibus imputatur, hic contra non fuit nisi posterius. Qui possunt igitur non duo esse distincti reatus, inter quos tot tantaque possunt notari discrimina?

Hinc patet sententiam Placei cum Decreto quatuor apud Helvetios civitatum Evangelicarum, quod Carentonensi D. Garissolius subiungit, minime pugnare. Nam vel Decretum Synodi Carentonianae laudant, cum quo Placei sententia, ut iam probavi, concordat; vel cur laudent rationem reddunt his paucissimis verbis: In Adamo enim et cum Adamo qui peccarunt, Adami illis peccatum merito imputatur — quam propositionem Placeus verissimam esse agnoscit. Aequum enim profecto est ut qui in et cum Adamo peccaverunt, his peccatum imputetur quod in eo et cum eo commiserunt. Communis peccati communem esse imputationem iustum est. Sed quid est nos in et cum Adamo peccasse? Peccatum Adami nobis imputari? Ita accipit D. Garissolius Cap. VIII. §. XXI. Quomodo enim, inquit, qui multis post saeculis extiterunt, iam antea in alio peccasse, nisi quia ille eum actum exercuit, qui posterorum ita reputatur, ac si ipsi illum commisissent? Et subiicit Theologos, cum docent nos in Christo satisfecisse, non aliud sibi velle, quam Christi satisfactionem nobis imputari. Congruit haec eius interpretatio cum eo quod saepe inculcat, peccatum Adami non nisi per imputationem nostrum esse. Hinc enim sequitur nos in et cum Adamo non peccasse nisi imputative. Sed sic doctissimorum Theologorum ratio evaderet nugatoria. Idem enim probarent per idem — imputationem peccati Adami per imputationem peccati Adami — quam nugationem, praesertim in tam gravi Decreto, illis tribuere nefas est. Quid ergo sibi vult illa phrasis? Id potest ex simili intelligi. Si quis enim diceret, nos in et cum Adamo fuisse, sensus esset, non Esse Adami nobis imputari, sed Esse Adami nobiscum per propagationem naturalem esse communicatum. Sic cum dicimur in et cum Adamo peccasse, sensus est, non peccatum Adami nobis imputari (id enim esset, ut dixi, nugationem in praestantissimorum virorum Decretum importare), sed peccatum Adami nobiscum per propagationem naturalem esse communicatum. Ex quo sequitur illud merito nobis imputari, sed imputatione mediata seu consequente, quam Placeus constanter agnoscit et tenet.
